It contains, at the founding of the church, a scene where the risen Christ is doubted by his own inner circle at point-blank range, and the doubter is not expelled, but I am saving that scene for the next chapter. The book kept surprising me by being on both sides of arguments I expected it to lose in one move. I had been told it was a hammer for settling questions. I found an anvil where questions get forged.

## The paragraph with my name in it

And then I hit Romans 1, and Romans 1 hit back, and I need to walk you through this carefully, because it is the passage that comes nearest to calling the man I was a liar, and if I dodge it I have broken my contract with you.

Paul, writing to the church in Rome around the late fifties of the first century, says this. For what can be known about God is plain to them, because God has shown it to them. For his invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made. So they are without excuse (Romans 1:19-20). And a verse earlier he has said how this can be, that the truth is being suppressed (Romans 1:18). Now, read that as the atheist I was. It is infuriating. It appears to say the thing I told you in chapter two I most despised, that unbelievers secretly know and are lying, the theory that calls you a coward and a liar in one breath while pretending to be generous. If Romans 1 means that every atheist is consciously concealing a belief in God, then Romans 1 is wrong about me, because I genuinely did not believe, all the way down, with my whole mind, and no text gets to overrule my own access to what I was.

But I no longer think that is what the paragraph is doing, and my reasons are in the text, not in my comfort. Follow Paul's argument past the part atheists get shown. The same passage indicts religion, immediately, the exchange of the glory of God for images (Romans 1:23), idols, the pious kind included, and then Paul rounds on the moralist at the start of the next chapter and tells him he is without excuse in the same breath, in the same words (Romans 2:1), and by the third chapter the trap has closed on everyone, none is righteous, no, not one (Romans 3:10). Do you see the shape? Suppression, in Paul's argument, is not a special crime of atheists. It is the universal human method, and the religious commit it with hymnals. Everyone takes the signal and manages it. The pagan turns it into statues, the moralist turns it into superiority, the churchgoer turns it into furniture, and the atheist turns it into aesthetics, files it, and keeps walking. When I finally read Romans 1 with the whole argument attached, I did not find the theory that atheists are liars. I found a description of a thing I had actually done and have shown you doing, for four chapters, in detail. I never once lied about believing. I managed the knock. I explained the address, filed the trembling, universalized the cold, and called the management maturity, and I did it, this is Paul's word and it earned itself, conveniently. The suppression was not a lie I told. It was a filing system I built, and I built it for the reason Paul names, because the alternative had a claim in it that would cost me the house.

> The suppression was not a lie I told. It was a filing system I built.

I want to be exact about what I am conceding and what I am not, because this is the page where a skeptical reader checks whether I have gone soft. I am not conceding that unbelievers secretly believe. They do not, and the Christian who deploys Romans 1 as a mind-reading device has read one paragraph of a three-chapter argument and should be handed the rest. I am conceding something that I think is both harder and fairer, that no one handles the data neutrally, that the believer and the unbeliever are both running managed portfolios, and that the direction of my management, all those years, ran exactly along the grain of my wound and my pride, precisely as Paul's account predicts and precisely as chapter three's arithmetic allows. Romans 1 did not call the man I was a liar. It called him a manager, and on the evidence of this book, the charge sticks.

What the native-born reader cannot feel, and what I cannot stop feeling, is how strange it is that the book knew. That is the report from the language school, the one finding under everything. I came to Scripture braced for propaganda and found, over and over, my own case file, the ache in Ecclesiastes, the flinch in Psalm 103, the filing system in Romans 1, written down centuries before I existed by men who had never met me and could not have, unless the claim at the center of the whole library is true, that there is one who knows the frame. I do not ask you to believe that yet. I ask you to do what I did, late, accented, without calluses. Read it as if you had never heard of it. It is not the book you were told it was. It was not the book I was told it was, and I was told by experts, and the experts, I have to report, had not read it recently either.
chapters.verdict: The suppression was not a lie I told. It was a filing system I built.
reflect: Is there a word that is broken in your mouth the way father was broken in Bell's? What, if anything, could repair it?
What have you been told the Bible is, and by whom? What would reading it at full strength, as an adult, look like?
Where in your own thinking do you manage evidence rather than face it, and how would you catch yourself doing it?

chapters.title: The Eighth Day of Thomas
chapters.summary: John 20 walked slowly. The demand for the marks, the eight days held without relenting, the wounds offered instead of a lecture, and a blessing aimed not at credulity but at the latecomers. The story indicts every community that handles its Thomases worse than its Lord did.
chapters.body:
Every institution tells you what it really is by what it keeps in its founding documents when it had every reason to cut. Institutions curate. Movements sand their origin stories smooth, and the early church had motive and opportunity to sand this one, a story in which the resurrection, the claim on which everything depends, is flatly disbelieved at point-blank range by a member of the inner circle, out loud, in terms an empiricist would sign. The church kept it. The church read it aloud for centuries while critics were already calling the whole thing credulous. I want to walk through that story slowly, because I am the kind of believer who exists because it was kept, and then I want to say what it indicts, which is not the skeptic.

## Unless I see

John 20. The disciples are locked in a room, for fear, the text says plainly, and the risen Jesus stands among them, and shows them his hands and his side, and they believe because they see (John 20:19-20). Mark that. The other ten got evidence, direct, physical, unsolicited evidence, before a single one of them believed. The tradition never calls the ten heroes of faith for this. It just records it.

Thomas was not there. And when the others tell him, we have seen the Lord, he gives the answer that made him a byword for two thousand years, and I will give it to you exactly, because it deserves exactness. Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and place my finger into the mark of the nails, and place my hand into his side, I will never believe (John 20:25). Look at what he is actually asking for. Not a sign in general, not a feeling, but the marks, specific, falsifiable, the scars in particular hands, evidence that the one standing before him is not a ghost, not a double, not grief hallucinating, but the same man who was crucified. It is a demand for continuity of identity, which is the exact scientific question, and notice too what he is refusing. He is refusing testimony. Ten of his closest friends, men he has lived beside for three years, tell him a thing in unison, and he says, in effect, your report is not my verification. That sentence could have been carved over the door of my atheism. I refused testimony for decades, and chapter six of this book told you I was partly right to, because testimony establishes the witnesses, not the fact.

So here is Thomas, the patron saint of everyone I used to drink coffee with, holding the line for eight days, and I want you to sit in those eight days with him, because the text makes them pass. Eight days inside a community that believes something you do not. Everyone around you glowing with a joy you cannot join and will not fake. If you have ever been the unbeliever at the family table, you know the eight days. They are long, and there is a temptation in them that no one names, the temptation to relent socially, to believe because the isolation aches, and the record shows Thomas did not take that exit, and I honor him for it. Belief obtained by social exhaustion would have been worthless, and he seems to have known it.

## The wounds offered

Then Jesus comes back. And this is where the story stops being about Thomas and starts being about the one he doubted, because watch the sequence. Jesus appears, and before Thomas says a word, Jesus repeats Thomas's own conditions back to him, the finger, the hands, the side, the private demand quoted verbatim by someone who was not in the room when it was made (John 20:27). The skeptic's challenge, it turns out, was heard. Not resented. Heard. And then, instead of the lecture Thomas has braced for, the wounds are offered. Put your finger here. As if to say, your test is accepted. Your criteria are not an insult to me. I will be verified by the marks of the worst thing that ever happened, because the marks are what I have instead of credentials. It is the only scene in any scripture of any faith I know where the deity submits to peer review.

The one sentence of correction is brief, and it is the hinge of the scene. Do not disbelieve, but believe (John 20:27). Notice what is not said. Not, how dare you. Not, you are no true disciple. The word is an invitation with a direction on it, stop leaning away, lean the other way, and it is issued while the evidence is being handed over, not instead of the evidence. And Thomas answers with the highest confession in the entire Gospel, calling him his Lord and his God (John 20:28). The empiricist, given his data, out-believes everyone in the building. No one in John's Gospel says anything stronger. The man who demanded the most ended by confessing the most, and I do not think that is an accident of the narrative. I think it is the narrative. The depth of a faith tends to match the depth of the questions that were allowed on the way in. Shallow permission, shallow confession. Thomas was permitted everything, so he could confess everything.

## The blessing over the shoulder

Then comes the line believers quote at skeptics, and I want to take it out of their hands gently, because it does not say what the quoters want it to say. Have you believed because you have seen me? (John 20:29), Jesus asks, and then he pronounces the greater blessing on those who will believe without having seen. Read flat-footed, it sounds like a demotion of evidence and a promotion of credulity, believe blind and be praised for it. But that reading collapses on the scene it sits in. Jesus has just spent the entire episode providing exactly the evidence Thomas demanded. If believing without evidence were the ideal, the offer of the wounds was a mistake, and the appearance to the other ten was a mistake, and the whole Gospel of John, which announces on its face that it was written as evidence so that you may believe (John 20:31), is a mistake. No. The blessing is not aimed over Thomas's head at some purer, less curious believer. It is aimed over his shoulder, at us, at every reader who arrives after the eyewitness generation is gone, who will never get the hands and the side, who must weigh testimony, which is a harder position, and the sentence names it as harder and blesses the people who will occupy it. It is not a rebuke of the empiricist. It is a mercy addressed to the latecomers, of whom I am one, and so, if you have read this far, are you.

## What the story indicts

So what does the story indict? Not doubt. The text will not support a single sentence against the doubter, and I have looked, the way you check the fine print of a contract you are about to sign. What the story indicts, quietly and forever, is every community that handles its Thomases worse than its Lord did. I say this now as clergy, from inside the institution, wearing its name. The church has spent much of my lifetime treating the skeptic's demand for evidence as an insult to be repelled instead of a criterion to be met, shaming the eight days instead of respecting them, quoting the blessing on the unseeing as a warrant for offering nothing to see. I have done it myself. There have been Sundays I answered a hard and honest question with the tone Jesus never once used on Thomas, and the person who asked it did not come back, and I remember them, specifically, by face. We built whole cultures of discipleship in which the man who says I will not believe until I see is handled as a problem, when the founding text handles him as a disciple, keeps his name on the list, waits out his eight days, and gives him the wounds.

The oldest documents of this faith keep a doubter in the founding circle. He was not sanded out. He was answered. Whatever else you conclude about the resurrection, and I know where you likely stand, and I stood there, that editorial decision tells you what this movement believed about people like you at the hour of its birth, before it had power, before it had anything to protect. It believed you belonged in the room for the eight days. It believed your conditions deserved to be heard rather than mocked. It believed the wounds could bear your inspection. A church that believes those three things again would be a church my old friends could at least walk into, and I am trying, one small congregation at a time, to be that church, because I was Thomas, and somebody kept a seat.
chapters.verdict: The founding circle kept a doubter. He was not sanded out. He was answered.
reflect: Thomas refused the unanimous testimony of ten close friends. Was he wrong to?
What conditions would you set, honestly, before believing a claim this large? Have you ever said them out loud?
If you have ever been the unbeliever at a believing table, what did the eight days feel like? What helped, and what made it worse?

chapters.title: The Atheist in the Pulpit
chapters.summary: Fifteen years at First Baptist Church of Fenton with the old atheist listening to every sermon. The pastors who confess their gray weeks through the Pastors Connection Network, and five sons repairing a broken word one generation downstream.
chapters.body:
There is an atheist in my pulpit every Sunday morning. He is not a visitor slipping in at the back. He is me, the man I was for most of my life, whose reasons I can still recite without notes, standing inside the man who now preaches. I lead First Baptist Church of Fenton, Michigan, a real congregation of real people in a real town, and I have been doing pastoral work for fifteen years, and in all that time the old man has never once left the building. This chapter is about what it is to do this work with him listening, because I have come to believe he is not a haunting. He is a colleague. He may be the most useful colleague I have.

## The listener in the second row

Understand what I mean, practically. Every sermon I write passes through him before it reaches anyone else. I will draft a sentence, some smooth confident sentence of the kind the trade produces by the yard, God never gives you more than you can handle, everything happens for a reason, and the man in the second row of my mind looks up from his Russell and says, do you know that, or does it just fill the silence? He caught me the first year and he catches me still. He cannot be preached at, because he has heard preaching and knows all its exits. He cannot be impressed by my office, because he watched me get it. The only thing he has ever responded to is the thing that was done to him, which is evidence handled honestly, wounds shown rather than credentials, and a speaker who is visibly inside his own indictment. So that is the sermon I try to write, every week, for him, on the theory that a sermon that can survive the man I was might be of some use to the people in the actual pews, who carry more of him inside them than they will ever tell a pastor.

Because they do. That is the open secret of the trade, the one the church talks about least and should talk about most. The pews are not full of believers and the street full of skeptics, with a wall between. The line runs through every chest in the building, mine included. The woman who organizes the meal train when someone is dying has a file of unanswered prayers she has stopped mentioning. The deacon who prays aloud better than I do buried a son twenty years ago and some part of him is still in the eighth day, waiting to see the hands. I know these things because fifteen years of hospital corridors and gravesides and marriages coming apart in my office have taught me what people actually carry, and what they carry is almost never clean belief or clean unbelief. It is the man in Mark 9, both clauses, in one breath. A church that admits this becomes a place where the clauses can be spoken. A church that denies it becomes a theater, and the performances are killing the performers, and I say that as a man who has done his seasons on that stage and felt what it costs.

## The pastors in the far country

The performance problem is what led me, eventually, to the other work I do. I founded the Pastors Connection Network because of a discovery I made that I was not looking for, which is that clergy are the loneliest professionals I have ever met, and that a startling amount of the loneliness is doctrinal. A pastor stands up every week as the designated believer, the one whose certainty the room borrows, and the role has no legal place to set anything down. Where does the designated believer go on the weeks the far side goes gray? Not to his elders, who employ him. Not always to his wife, who has her own weeks. And so it built itself, network of men and women who tell each other the truth, and I will tell you the strange credential that made me, of all people, a safe address for some of them. It is that I was an atheist, openly, in print, and became a pastor anyway, which means a pastor can say to me the sentence he can say nowhere else, some weeks I do not know if any of it is true, and watch my face and find nothing there but recognition. I have heard that sentence, or its cousins, more times than I could count. These are not frauds. They are Thomases in a profession that pays them to be Peters, and the eight days come for them like they come for everyone, and the only pastoral care most of them have ever received for it is the advice to try harder, which is the one strategy the actual Thomas conspicuously did not need.

What do I tell them? What I have told you, mostly. That belief is trust across a gap, not the gap's abolition. That the flinch can be the prayer. That the founding documents keep a doubter in the founding circle, answered rather than shamed. And that their doubt, handled honestly, is not the enemy of their people, it may be the only fully honest gift they have, because a shepherd who has personally wintered in the far country does not lead the flock by hearsay.

## Five sons and a broken word

And then there is the other congregation, the one that lives in my house. I am raising five sons. I want you to feel the arithmetic of that the way I feel it at the kitchen table. A man who grew up with an empty chair now sits at the head of a table with five boys at it, and the word father, the most defective word in his dictionary, the word he learned to pray through a flinch, is what they call him. It is the plainest fact of my life and I have never once gotten used to it.

Here is what fatherhood did that nothing else could do, not the crossing, not the pulpit, not the books. It moved me to the other end of the road. All my life I had known the road from one position, the boy watching it, then the boy refusing to watch it, then the man reading about a father who watched it and coming apart. Now I am the father, and I find that the watching is not a discipline. It is a reflex. When one of my sons is late, something in me stands up and goes to the window, without a decision, and the first time I caught myself doing it I had to sit down, because I understood, in my body, what Luke 15:20 had been claiming all along, that seeing him a long way off is simply what a father's eyes do, that the boy on the road in the dark all those years ago was wrong about the nature of fatherhood, not wrong to grieve his own father, that grief was correct, but wrong to universalize him. I had taken one man's failure and written it into the constitution of the universe. My sons are teaching me the amendment.

I am not the proof of anything, I want to be careful here. I am a man with a temper I watch, and a schedule that eats what it should not, and there are evenings I fail those boys in ordinary ways and lie awake doing the old arithmetic. But they will not grow up with the axiom. Whatever else my sons carry out of my house, they will not carry the sentence fathers do not come, because they have a father who comes, imperfectly, daily, on purpose, and who tells them why. I tell them about their grandfather, without bitterness, because they deserve the truth of where they come from. And I tell them about the other Father, the one I met late, and when I teach them to pray the word I once could not say, they say it without any flinch at all, easily, the way you speak your first language, and I stand behind them with my eyes shut, hearing the sound of a broken word being repaired one generation downstream. That sound is most of what I know about redemption. Not the wound undone. The wound refused passage.

The atheist in the pulpit watches all of this, the sermons he edits, the pastors who confess to me because of him, the table with the five boys. And I will tell you the strangest thing about our long cohabitation. I no longer want him gone. For years I prayed to be rid of him, thinking him the residue of the far country, and slowly I understood that he is something else. He is the man the Father ran at. Delete him and I delete the running. He is the reason I cannot lie in the pulpit, cannot shame a doubter, cannot preach a certainty I am not carrying, cannot treat one lost sheep as a rounding error. He was kept, I have come to believe, the way the wounds were kept. Risen bodies, notice, retain their scars, the marks were the verification, the worst thing became the credential. I am not risen yet. But the scar is already working.
chapters.verdict: The wound was not undone. It was refused passage.
reflect: Who in your life is allowed to hear the sentence, some weeks I do not know if any of it is true? If no one, what does that cost?
What broken word are you carrying, and who is downstream of it?
Does it change your read of the church to learn that the line between belief and doubt runs through the pews and the pulpit alike?

chapters.title: To the Man on the Other Side
chapters.summary: The letter to the man he was. Taylor's cross-pressure lowering the temperature on both sides, three requests that require no belief, the clause about gentleness and respect, and an ending left where Luke left his. On the porch, with the door open.
chapters.body:
Every chapter of this book has been addressed to you, but through a story, and now the story is told and it is just the two of us. You, the reader who is where I was, and me, owing you an ending that does not cheat. I have thought a long time about what the last chapter of this book is allowed to be. It is not allowed to be an altar call, because I promised no collar-grabbing and I have watched what manufactured urgency does to honest people, it inoculates them. It is not allowed to be a victory lap, because I did not win, I told you, I lost. What it is allowed to be, I think, is the letter I would write to the man I was, if letters could travel that direction, and you are allowed to read it over his shoulder, and where it does not fit you, drop it, because you are not him. You are someone I have never met, standing in a room I have never seen, and the worst habit of religious writers is pretending otherwise.

## The weather on both sides of the line

First, something I learned from a philosopher, because it will lower the temperature of everything that follows. Charles Taylor, in A Secular Age, in 2007, spent nine hundred pages on a question nobody had asked properly, which is not whether God exists but why belief in God, which was simply the air in the year 1500, became one option among others by the year 2000, and a contested option at that. And the most useful thing in all those pages, for you and me, is his description of how it actually feels to live now. He calls it cross-pressure. The believer today lives with the pressure of doubt inside his belief, he cannot help knowing his faith is deniable, the secular account sits in the pew with him. And the unbeliever lives with the pressure of transcendence inside his unbelief, moments when the closed world feels too small for what just happened to him, music, birth, grief, the hard clear sky, and he cannot help knowing his account is deniable too. Nobody, Taylor says, gets to stand on solid ground and watch the other side wobble. The wobble is the age. It is the weather over every position, and the fundamentalist and the village atheist are the two men most committed to denying the forecast.

I hand you that finding for one reason. It means your doubts about your unbelief, the ones this book has maybe surfaced, the ache, the address, the door that will not stay shut, are not symptoms of weakness, and my doubts inside my faith are not symptoms of fraud. They are what intellectual honesty feels like from the inside, now, on both sides of the line. So you do not owe anyone a performance of certainty, and you should not trust anyone performing one at you, in either direction. That includes clergy. That includes the confident atheists of the podcast circuit. That includes, on his bad days, the author of this book.

## What I ask of you

Now, the letter. Here is what I would say to the man with the Russell on his shelf and the file cabinet in his chest, and I know how he receives things, so it is short, and none of it requires him to believe anything.

Press on the strangeness. That is the whole request. You have a theory of the ache, I had it too, and it is a good theory, and I will go to my grave saying so. But you have never audited it, because it has never had a rival in your house. So audit. Find the hunger your explanation explains but never once reduces, and instead of filing it, sit with it long enough to notice whether it behaves like a misfire or like a signal. Ask why the explanation has to be reapplied every time, like a paint that will not cure. That is not what true explanations usually require. You know that. You are the one who taught me to notice things like that.

Then audit the certainty itself, the way you audit everyone else's. Ask how much of it is reasoning and how much is the shape of the room you are standing in, and whether the room has a wound in it, as mine did. I am not saying your unbelief is your wound. I spent a whole chapter refusing that move and I refuse it here. I am saying you have a cost sheet, everyone does, and you have never read yours, and a man who will not read his own cost sheet is not yet the empiricist he believes himself to be.

And read the primary texts. This one is almost unfair, because it costs an evening and it is the request my whole guild has failed to make sound serious. You have opinions about a book you have not read recently, or ever, not really, not as an adult, not at full strength. Read Luke 15 yourself, alone, slowly, and watch what the father does, and check whether the story you were told about this religion survives contact with the story the religion actually tells. Read the eighth day of Thomas. Read Ecclesiastes and find out who kept your complaint in their canon. You are not agreeing to anything. You are doing what the men on your own shelf would do, going to the source before ruling on it.

That is all. Notice what is not on the list. I am not asking you to pray, the experiment is rigged in both directions and we both know it. I am not asking you to attend anything. I am not asking you to want this to be true, wanting was never the mechanism, I was wanting it false the whole way across. The pressure you are braced for is not coming, and not because I am above applying it, but because I sat where you sit, and I know that it does not work, and I know that it is disrespect wearing kindness, and there is a sentence in the New Testament, of all places, that forbids it to me. Always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you, Peter writes, and then the clause my tribe keeps forgetting is in the verse, yet do it with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). With gentleness. With respect. The manner is not a tactic bolted onto the message. It is required by the message, because the message says you are not a target, you are the one the story is about, and nobody chases the one the story is about into a corner.

## The porch

I keep coming back to the way Luke leaves it, and I have decided the way Luke leaves it is the way I have to leave it, because the storyteller knew something about endings that the conversion genre forgot. The parable of the two sons does not end. The younger son is inside, the music is playing, and the elder brother is standing on the porch with his arithmetic, and the father has come out, again, the second time in one evening, and made his case, and the last thing we see is the two of them out there in the dark with the door open. No resolution. Luke does not tell us whether the elder brother ever goes in, because the people that brother was drawn from were still standing in front of Jesus, deciding, and the story had the manners to leave the decision where it lived, with them.

I have been every man in that story now. I was the younger son in the far country, doing the math on what I deserved. I was the elder brother for years, though my porch was a library, keeping accounts against a father I refused to know. Now, strangest of all, I spend my working life as a small and failing image of the father, watching roads, going out to porches, leaving the music to stand in the dark with whoever cannot come in yet, and I can tell you from the father's end what I could never see from the porch. The door is not a trap. The music is not a performance staged to lure you. And the man who came out to stand with you is not going back in without you because the feast, and this is the thing I did not know, the feast is not complete while the porch is occupied. That is what all the running was about, in the story and in my life. Not the recovery of an asset. The setting of a table that has your chair at it, and has had, all along, which is either the oldest manipulation in the world or the plainest fact in it, and this book was never going to be able to decide that for you. It was only ever going to get you out onto the porch, where the two accounts can finally be told apart, because the music is audible from there.

So I will not end by telling you somebody is watching the road, although I believe it, and although I wrote it once before and meant it. I will end further down and quieter. You have a file, somewhere in the cabinet, thicker than the others, the one labeled with whatever you call the ache. One evening, not for me, take it out and read it as if another man had written it, and ask the question I would not ask for twenty years, the only question this whole book has been. What if it is not a file? What if it is a letter, and it has been arriving your whole life, and the reason it never stops coming is that the sender does not know how to stop? You will say the evidence is insufficient to decide. Maybe. I said that too, in this very room, at this hour of the night. The porch is quiet. The door is open. I am not going to tell you what to do with that.

I am going to tell you what I did.

I stopped explaining the music.
